title: Lecture 7. Unstructured Interview
summary:
1 What is an unstructured interview

2 Application in an educational organization

1. What is an unstructured interview An unstructured interview is methodologically the simplest and most basic diagnostic method compared to all others. Historically, since this method largely developed within the psychoanalytic tradition, it is also called a clinical or in-depth interview.

Unlike a journalistic interview, whose goal is to gather as much information as possible about something, an unstructured interview is conducted to make a final judgment. Doctors make a conclusion — sick or not sick. Investigators make a conclusion — guilty or not guilty. In clinical practice, this is a diagnostic judgment in accordance with the signs of a certain illness; in legal practice, it is the qualification of an act in accordance with a specific article of the code.

The clinical interview process includes observing the patient and interpreting their behavior (slips of the tongue, omissions, psychodynamic tension, resistance, etc.). Therefore, such an interview does not have a plan or structure as such: questions are asked not from the perspective of their logical sequence, but from the perspective of the shortest path to a categorical judgment, which is built along the way, taking into account the results of observation and interpretation of the interviewee's behavior.

Nevertheless, doctors have a list of questions, the answers to which the doctor must somehow obtain to make a diagnosis. Typically, during an interview, psychiatrists ask the following questions:

Description of current state and mental status — consciousness (person, time, place), — contact features, patient's attitude to their condition, adequacy of assessment, — mood, affective background, — hallucinatory-delusional symptoms (presence of delusions, sensory deception), — features of perception, thinking. — personality and characterological features, — behavioral features (behavioral pattern). Life history (significant moments). Anamnesis of the disease (first symptoms, their development, seeking help). In case of a narcological referral, anamnesis from the first trial. Questions about heredity. Diagnostic hypothesis. External manifestations: tension, resistance, evasion, agitation. 2. Application in an educational organization In the practice of an educational organization, the unstructured interview method is primarily used by educational psychologists during individual counseling. Here, the same tasks are solved as in any research — to obtain information about the problem the student has approached with, its causes and manifestations, by asking relevant questions during the conversation. In other words, whether the specialist realizes it or not, during the session, they construct a theoretical model of the client's problem in their mind.

Based on the diagnostic part of the consultation, the specialist makes judgments about the correctness or incorrectness of hypotheses that emerged during the consultation, about the true scope and causes of the problem the student has approached with. However, unlike medical practice, the content and logic of the psychologist's questions are determined not by clinical notions of mental illnesses, as in the example given above, but by the logic of the counseling model adhered to by the educational psychologist. For example, a proponent of the cognitive-behavioral approach will analyze the client's behavior, paying attention to cognitive distortions, emotional reactions, and the logic of the client's actions related to the problem.

It should be noted that the unstructured interview has its undeniable advantages in an educational organization, compared to other diagnostic methods:

provides a very high degree of reliability of results, compared, for example, to psychological testing; can include any range of questions, whereas psychological tests are aimed at assessing a limited range of situations and problems; includes observation of the interviewee and takes into account the context of the situation; in many cases, it is more economical than psychological testing (considering the time required to organize its conduct and process the results). Main disadvantages of an unstructured interview:

high requirements for specialist qualifications, impossibility of simultaneously examining a large number of people, subjectivity of assessment. The results of an unstructured interview are recorded as answers to key questions in the form of a conclusion, which usually includes: formal socio-demographic data, a description of the reason for referral, a description of behavioral features, identified problems and their causes, confirmed diagnostic hypotheses, and recommendations. In some cases, a full transcript of the interview text is made for research purposes.

In an educational organization, the results of individual psychological counseling, during which an unstructured interview is effectively used, are recorded in the form of reporting that does not necessarily involve preparing a full conclusion, but only recording key indicators in the reporting documentation.
